Why DC bias analysis matters

The operating point determines whether a MOSFET can act as a switch, current source, or amplifier.

Beginner foundation

DC means the circuit has settled to a constant operating condition

In a DC analysis, voltages and currents do not vary with time. Capacitors are treated as open circuits after transients, inductors as shorts in ideal steady state, and the MOSFET is represented by a region-dependent current-voltage equation.

Bias

Intentional DC voltages and currents that place a transistor at a useful operating point.

Q-point

The quiescent values \((I_D,V_{GS},V_{DS})\) before an AC signal is applied.

Region

The operating mode - cutoff, triode, or saturation - that determines which device equation is valid.

Connection to Module 4

Module 4 supplied the first-order nMOS equations. Module 5 adds the surrounding resistors and voltage sources. The actual operating point must satisfy both the MOSFET equation and all circuit laws at the same time.

\[ \text{device equation} + \text{KCL/KVL constraints} \longrightarrow \text{DC operating point} \]
Source-based scope: the examples, numerical values, figures, and main progression are taken from the uploaded Module 5 PDF. The expanded explanations, interactive solvers, error checks, and beginner design guidance are supplemental instructional material.

Learning objectives

After completing the module, students should be able to:

2

3

4

Check current direction, voltage bounds, overdrive, and region validity.
5

Determine which transistor conducts and solve the output using symmetry or a single-device reduction.

Topic 5.1

DC Analysis Mindset: Unknowns, Equations, and Region Checks

Build a repeatable procedure before solving individual circuits.

Section introduction

A MOSFET equation cannot be chosen until a region is assumed

The difficulty of MOSFET DC analysis is not Ohm's law. It is that the device equation changes with the unknown terminal voltages. The reliable solution is conditional reasoning: assume a region, solve the corresponding circuit, then verify that the result belongs to that region.

Known quantities

Supply voltages, resistor values, gate-bias networks, threshold voltage, device parameter \(k_n\), and sometimes channel-length modulation \(\lambda\).

Typical unknowns

\(I_D\), \(V_G\), \(V_S\), \(V_D\), \(V_{GS}\), \(V_{DS}\), overdrive \(V_{OV}\), and region of operation.

Source Figure: Region map and output characteristics

Extracted from Module 5 PDF · page 1
Extensive beginner theory

The five-step assume-solve-verify loop

If you are new to MOSFET circuits, think of this method as a roadmap. First name the voltages, then use the gate-current rule, then choose one transistor mode, connect it to the surrounding resistor network, and finally check whether your answer is physically allowed.

Label every node and polarity. Write \(V_{GS}=V_G-V_S\) and \(V_{DS}=V_D-V_S\). Do not assume the source is grounded unless the circuit shows it.
Use the insulated-gate fact. In the ideal DC model, \(I_G\approx0\). A resistor divider connected only to the gate is therefore essentially unloaded.
Assume a region and write one device equation. Use cutoff, triode, or saturation — never mix equations from different regions in the same trial.
Apply KCL, KVL, and resistor relations. Convert all node voltages to functions of the same unknown, often \(I_D\).
Solve and verify. Test the exact inequalities. If they fail, discard that solution and repeat with another region.
Assumed regionnMOS conditionFirst-order current equationPhysical picture
Cutoff\(V_{GS}\le V_T\)\(I_D\approx 0\)No strong inversion channel.
Triode\(V_{GS}>V_T\), \(0\le V_{DS}<V_{OV}\)\(I_D=k_n\left(V_{OV}V_{DS}-\frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right)\)Continuous channel; voltage-controlled resistor behavior.
Saturation\(V_{GS}>V_T\), \(V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}\)\(I_D=\frac{1}{2}k_nV_{OV}^2\)Channel pinches off near the drain; current is mainly gate controlled.

Why verification is mandatory

A quadratic equation can produce multiple roots. Only roots that obey the assumed region, voltage limits, and current direction are physical.

Why saturation is often tried first

Analog bias circuits usually intend the MOSFET to behave as a gate-controlled current source. Saturation gives the simplest current equation.

Gate current versus drain current

\(I_G\approx0\) does not mean \(I_D=0\). The gate controls channel charge electrostatically while drain current flows through the channel.

Power and safety checks

After solving, calculate \(P_D=V_{DS}I_D\) and resistor powers. A mathematically valid point may exceed a component rating.

Common beginner errors

  • Using \(V_G\) in place of \(V_{GS}\).
  • Declaring saturation merely because the device is ON.
  • Keeping both quadratic roots without checking them.
  • Forgetting that a source resistor makes \(V_S=I_DR_S\), reducing \(V_{GS}\).
  • Using volts, amperes, ohms, milliamperes, and kilohms inconsistently.

PPT Circuit 4 · Example 5.5

Fixed-Gate nMOS Triode Design

Design \(R_D\) for a small drain voltage and calculate effective \(R_{DS}\).

Slides 22–25

Use the triode equation when \(V_{DS}<V_{OV}\)

With the source grounded, \(V_{GS}=V_G\) and \(V_{DS}=V_D\). The target \(V_D\) must be compared with \(V_{OV}=V_G-V_T\) before selecting the equation.

Current

\[I_D=k_n\left(V_{OV}V_{DS}-\frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right)\]

Design

\[R_D=\frac{V_{DD}-V_D}{I_D},\qquad R_{DS,eff}=\frac{V_D}{I_D}\]

Example 2

nMOS Divider Bias with Source Degeneration

The source resistor creates negative feedback and makes the current equation implicit.

Section introduction

The gate divider sets voltage; the source resistor lets the transistor correct its own current

Because the ideal gate draws almost no DC current, \(R_{G1}\) and \(R_{G2}\) set \(V_G\) independently of the MOSFET. But \(V_S=I_DR_S\), so any increase in current raises the source voltage and reduces \(V_{GS}=V_G-V_S\). This is negative feedback.

Source Figure: Divider-biased nMOS with drain and source resistors

Extracted from Module 5 PDF · page 4
Extensive beginner derivation

Turn a multi-node circuit into one equation in \(I_D\)

Use the unloaded divider: \(V_G=V_{DD}R_{G2}/(R_{G1}+R_{G2})\).
Express the source voltage as \(V_S=I_DR_S\).
Write \(V_{GS}=V_G-I_DR_S\) and \(V_{OV}=V_G-I_DR_S-V_T\).
Assume saturation and substitute into \(I_D=\tfrac12k_n(V_G-I_DR_S-V_T)^2\).
Solve the nonlinear equation. Reject negative current and any root that makes \(V_{GS}\le V_T\).
Find \(V_D=V_{DD}-I_DR_D\) and \(V_{DS}=V_D-V_S\).
Verify \(V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}\). If it fails, solve with the triode equation.

Why source degeneration stabilizes current

Suppose temperature or device variation tries to increase \(I_D\). The larger current increases \(V_S=I_DR_S\), which decreases \(V_{GS}\) and overdrive. That reduction opposes the original increase. This feedback improves bias stability at the cost of voltage headroom.

Divider current

\(I_{div}=V_{DD}/(R_{G1}+R_{G2})\). The same current flows through both divider resistors because \(I_G\approx0\).

Drain and source branch current

With no other branch at drain or source, \(I_{RD}=I_D=I_{RS}\).

Voltage headroom

Both \(R_D\) and \(R_S\) consume supply voltage. Excessive current can force \(V_D<V_S\), which is outside the intended NMOS orientation.

Physical root

A root is acceptable only if current is nonnegative, node voltages are plausible, and the region check succeeds.

Unit shortcut used in the simulator

When current is in mA and resistance is in kΩ, their product is directly in volts: \((\text{mA})(\text{k}\Omega)=\text{V}\). This makes the feedback equations easier to inspect.

Module 5 Summary and Problem-Solving Guide

Organize every DC problem around terminal voltages, circuit constraints, and verification.

Wrap-up

The circuit determines terminal voltages; terminal voltages determine the MOSFET region

Do not memorize each example as a special case. Reduce every network to the same reasoning loop and use the transistor orientation to define the correct voltage polarities.

Universal workflow

Checklist for any MOSFET DC circuit

Identify nMOS or pMOS and mark gate, drain, source, and body.
Write terminal voltages explicitly from node voltages.
Use \(I_G\approx0\) to simplify gate-bias networks.
Assume cutoff, triode, or saturation.
Write only the equation for that assumed region.
Use KCL/KVL to reduce the circuit to one or more equations.
Solve numerically or algebraically and list all candidate roots.
Reject roots that violate current direction, voltage bounds, or region conditions.
Calculate all requested node voltages and branch currents.
Check power, resistor values, and design sensitivity.
Circuit patternPrimary simplificationTypical unknownKey verification
Gate-drain connected nMOS\(V_{GS}=V_{DS}\)Current, node voltage, or series resistorIf ON, saturation is automatic for positive \(V_T\)
Gate divider + source resistor\(V_G\) from unloaded divider; \(V_S=I_DR_S\)Implicit \(I_D\)Check \(V_{DS}\ge V_{OV}\) after solving
pMOS high-side biasUse \(V_{SG}\), \(V_{SD}\), and \(|V_{TP}|\)Gate divider and drain resistor\(V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{TP}|\)
Complementary common-source pairDetermine which device is ONOutput voltage from KCLCheck both device regions, KCL, and symmetry

Bridge to small-signal analysis

Once \(I_D\) is known, later modules can compute \(g_m\) and \(r_o\). An incorrect DC Q-point produces an incorrect amplifier model.

Bias versus signal

DC establishes the operating point. A small AC signal then moves the transistor around that point without ideally changing the assumed region.

Design tolerance

Threshold, \(k\), and resistor values vary. Source degeneration and feedback reduce sensitivity but consume voltage headroom.

Simulation discipline

A SPICE result is useful only when you can explain the region, current path, and approximate magnitude from hand analysis.

Final sanity checks

  • Every node voltage should lie within physically available rails unless a dependent source permits otherwise.
  • Resistor current direction must agree with its voltage drop.
  • An ON nMOS needs \(V_{GS}>V_T\); an ON pMOS needs \(V_{SG}>|V_{TP}|\).
  • Saturation and triode inequalities must use source-referenced voltages.
  • Total power delivered by supplies should equal total absorbed power within rounding.
